Frontier Fade.name: Frontier Fade
Frontier Fade.basicInfo:
The misted rim of The Still Frontier — the line where willed ground becomes unwilled. Ground grows indistinct here, colors wash toward grey, and sound carries strangely; walk far enough and the world simply stops, not with a wall but with a fading. Snow travels into the Fade and stops moving. The constant, faint sensation is that standing here is standing at the edge of someone's attention.

Living Ecology: Frost-tail fox tracks become constellations at the rim before fading, and unmoving snow hangs over root nurseries waiting for the next safe outward growth. The last conifers lean inward rather than toward nonexistent wind.
Frontier Fade.hiddenInfo:
The Fade advances as the Demi-Plane's ambient potential seeps outward and retreats when its mana runs low — the Chamberlain reads its position as the dimension's health report. The fade-line is unstable within Reach's own limits: objects left in it change; travelers who linger too long report their footprints fading before them, in the direction ahead rather than behind. Frozen shrines stand inside the Fade's reach — iced mid-ceremony, abandoned by no one known — and strange weather pockets hold their ground in its mists: one small snow that has never fallen is always just beginning here. The Fade is where expansion will begin when the creator chooses; the frontier always leaves a little room at the rim first, as if thinking ahead on its own.

Ecological Continuity: Frozen shrines and ceremonial-looking ice forms are natural crystallizations of Tsukiko's realm-memory unless play establishes a maker. They do not add lost inhabitants to the young plane.

Frostpine Ridge.name: Frostpine Ridge
Frostpine Ridge.basicInfo:
The high spine of The Still Frontier — a ridgeline of pale conifers with frost-glinting needles beneath a paler sky, under weather that is not quite weather: silver breath-mist, snow falling in slow spirals, frost-formed foxfire burning statically in the branches. Crest views give back the whole northern dimension; the furred sound is layered winter hush. Pale wolves and frost foxes pace here, watching travelers with an owner's calm rather than hunger.

Living Ecology: Glass-antler elk open migration lanes between pale trunks, spiral owls ride upward snow, and blue lace-fungus turns fallen frostwood into warm soil beneath the ice.
Frostpine Ridge.hiddenInfo:
The ridge is the frontier's oldest ground: its pale conifers were the dimension's first attempt to create weather and have not stopped since. Cave mouths thread beneath the root systems — cold hollows lined with frozen foxfire, some stretching back under the ridge into pockets of unmelted ice that hold mana like clear stone. Snow wraiths roost along the crest in settled weather; their paths mark the safest route across the scree. The Chamberlain visits twice a year and leaves a small frozen foxfire offering at a shrine none of his records mention building.

Ecological Continuity: The unrecorded-looking shrine is a foxfire-and-root formation produced by the region's memory of reverence. The Chamberlain's offerings acknowledge the place; they do not prove another population built it.

Ghost Valleys.name: Ghost Valleys
Ghost Valleys.basicInfo:
The shallow valleys of The Pale Reaches, filled with glowing silver fog that never fully settles or fully lifts. The valley floors shift texture without changing shape, and the fog gives back shapes: lanes, rooftops, lights, faces — a place seems to have been here before, then was not. Walking one valley end to end is never quite the same walk twice.

Living Ecology: Fogmice and pearl-foot hares leave temporary tracks across miniature landscapes that complete a season before noon. Veil skates graze silver spores inches above the valley floor.
Ghost Valleys.hiddenInfo:
The valley mist is raw dimensional potential in semi-tangible form — the Reaches' heart of the unspent. Uncontrolled, it forms fleeting ghost-landscapes that dissolve in seconds, sometimes matching places the creator has seen or dreamed; it has twice produced a doorway street that appears on no floor plan anywhere. Fog elementals condense from the densest mist: patient, watchful, and dissolving peacefully when entertained or ignored with equal confidence. Pale stone beasts stand among the benches like statuary until approached, then walk away precisely as if they had somewhere to be. The valleys have no memory of anyone's visit: footprints cool and fade within the hour.

Ecological Continuity: Focused intention shapes raw mist, while uncontrolled formations remain filtered by lichen and wildlife into harmless temporary ecology. They reveal remembered forms, not secret truth or prophecy.

Silver-Lichen Flats.name: Silver-Lichen Flats
Silver-Lichen Flats.basicInfo:
The broad benches of The Pale Reaches — white-grey stone terraces washed in silver lichen that lights faintly like constellations underfoot. By day the flats look austere; by night they glow in slow constellations that reform between one glance and the next. Pale crystals collect in the bench hollows where the fog pools overnight, and the whole flat has the settled patience of a place prepared in advance for something that has not yet been decided.

Living Ecology: Constellation lichen brightens beneath stoneback grazers and dims after releasing spores into the dawn fog. Each broad bench resembles a night sky laid level underfoot.
Silver-Lichen Flats.hiddenInfo:
The lichen's constellations are not random — they form the same arrangements of light twice a season, patterns the Chamberlain has charted and cannot decode. He believes they are the potential deciding what it will be, written faintly ahead of time. Silver lichen is the region's most valuable resource: a natural mana-conductive coating for warded surfaces that no artificer has learned to imitate. Temporary creatures made of potential occasionally cross the flats in perfect daylight, and travelers' brief structures — a camp, a bridge, a well — sometimes surface in the bench hollows after fog-heavy nights, half-complete, the potential rehearsing invention.

Ecological Continuity: Lichen patterns map local moisture and potential density rather than fate. Reading them can guide harvest and travel, never grant automatic knowledge of distant events.
